pages.transcription:
Ossining, July 25th, 41
Dear Hanna & Manfred, I just received your letter of June 26th
and a letter from mother of July 18th. I hope you are both
still in Bath, and probably there are some visitors with
you. I hope Marta got permission to come and spend a good long
holiday, although I have a suspicion that she won't be able
to resist the temptation of bottling fruit and vegetables. -
I am very happy that you are now really convinced that Eva
is in best, loving care and in surroundings which are just
what you think right. She thoroughly enjoys the holidays
and although she always wants us to visit her often and
long, she is not too eager to spend whole days away from
Amity Hall - which I think is a very good sign and should
greatly reassure you for the case that we should really
go to Brazil. Elizabeth who will come for tea next week
with part or the whole of her family has invited Eva for
a few days the week after, and although she likes to
go there she says she does not want to be away from
Amity Hall for long. I shall probably go over and see
Eva to-day, because for the weekend we shall have the
visit of Dr. Bondi - one of those many Bondis you disliked
mother to tell stories about. We have seen him quite
frequently recently in his business quality and as he was
very nice and helpful and reassuring Stefan wanted
to let him have the pleasure of a weekend out of town.
He has a clear logic lawyer's mind, and that is good against
Stefan's too productive imagination sometimes, and although
he is as ugly as Marks he seems to be quite nice. -
Our plans are still undecided but it looks as if in
the end we will go to Brazil. In any case we are bound
to come to a decision very soon and that will end this
disagreeable state of indecision and continued considerations
what to do best and why and when and where next to go.
pages.notes: Handschriftlicher Brief von Lotte Zweig. Tinte auf Papier.

pages.transcription:
By the way, a friend of ours, Camille Honig, a young Jewish
journalist who has been in Australia for some Jewish-British
war collections is returning to England shortly. We would
have loved to send you something through him, but when
we met him last it looked as if he would go by clipper,
and so we just asked him to ring you up as soon as he
arrives in London and promised him that you would
invite him for a weekend to Bath should you not be in
London just then. You will like him. He comes somewhere
from the Eastern Ghettos, has worked his way up and knows
a lot about art and literature. He is married to a non-Jewish
wife of a good English family, and has left her here with a
few months old baby. We have been together several times,
and I am sure you would like to get direct news from us
just as I would be happy to meet someone who just
spent some time with you. We had a letter from him
yesterday that he will probably sail in a few days, so
it will take weeks at the best before he can call you up.
He returns because he has to enlist for military service,
and I hope he will have time to see you. - Don't worry
that my treatment is still going on, it was meant to be so
from the beginning. The injections have been reduced
to once a week now and I am getting the top dosis of
1ccm. Gradually they will be given once a fortnight
and once a month only and after 6 or 12 months
it will be stopped and then I am supposed to be immune
against asthma. In any case I am quite well now, just
as I was the last years, and if I had some disagreeable
weeks, I have learned again to appreciate deeply the
fact of mere physical health. And once we shall have
settled down somewhere for more than two months,
be it here or in Brazil we shall be quite happy again.
Nothing is worse in the long run than being undecided,
and that is what we have been too long now, always
waiting for the next weeks to bring solutions from outside.

2) I hope you wrote a little in detail about your exam
Manfred! All I know is that you expected it to be dif-
ficult and that it required lots of time and studies.
Did you find the examinations difficult, were there
many others with you, were they all doctors already prac-
tising, and how many of them passed? Do you try to
get a hospital job now, and how are the chances? Or do
you expect to be called up soon? And will it be in your
quality as specialist do you think? - Do tell us about
all this as well as about your progress in chess and piano,
and never be afraid of writing too long letters. -
I was interested to hear that Edith Hoffman has married,
and surprised that her job at the Burlington still is
in existence. - We had Wilmot's letter and only expect
some information about the securities which have mean-
while been recalled by the Treasury, before answering
his questions which are very easy to answer once you
managed to understand his rather complicated way of
writing. - We continue to work hard, Stefan much harder
than I do for I stick to my principle never to work
after dinner if I can help it and he works until late.
My household does not take much time on the whole. I
make the menu, order everything by phone except the
meat which I like to see and for which I walk over
to the butchers 5 minutes from here, and the maid
does the cleaning and cooking. It is enjoyable to be
able to choose in which room to go and to have a room
of my own for my work, complete even with writing table.
Sometimes I occupy myself with the garden which con-
sists in mowing the lawn, and then I always remember
William and how we used to wonder that it took him so
long to mow those two terraces. Lots of wild rabbits help
to keep the grass short and they are amusing to watch and
I am glad that I have not to eat them as one of our guests
suggested.

I wonder how Marks' photographs of you, Manfred
and Rosemount turned out and I am impatient to have
them. It will be only a poor substitute for being with
you and talking with you, but there seems to be hope
that some day in some distant future we will be together
again - and how much will we have to talk and how
many nights will we have to sit at the fireplace until
far after midnight to get everything talked over!
Kindest regards to all and best love & kisses
to you
Lotte.

Dear Hannah & Manfred, we are not yet decided
what to do and you will hear soon of us.
I am rather depressed - This life without
a real home, this wandering around makes
me melancholic and it relaxes as this would
go on for years and years. Lotte feels much
better and I would wish a better husband for
her. I have done my autobiography till
to my fiftieth year and I am wondering
if I shall continue because the third
part would be rather sad and oppressive
We had here a very quiet time; I have
worked the whole day and Lotte looks al-
ready much better. Kindest regards Stefan
